text: How to use this guide

This guide teaches you to rebuild every Deneb chart in the **DenebShowcase** report from an empty visual. The goal is not just to copy specs but to understand them well enough to build your own charts.
Each chart chapter follows the same pattern:

items: **What you'll build** — the finished chart and the Power BI fields it needs.
**Steps** — the chart is built in 4–6 small steps. Each step tells you exactly what to add and where, explains *why* it works, and shows a picture of the result at that point.
**Every step is saved as a file** in `tableau-to-powerbi/tutorial/steps/` (e.g. `ch01_heatmap_step3.json`). If you get lost, paste that file into the Deneb editor and carry on.
**Check your understanding** — small exercises to try on your own.

text: Chapters 1–4 are the foundations. Read them first even if you are in a hurry: every chart chapter assumes them. Chapters 5–11 are the Tableau-style charts (pages 1–2 of the report), chapters 12–15 the NYT-style charts (pages 3–5). Appendices cover troubleshooting and a quick reference.

Work inside the DenebShowcase report: it already has all the tables and measures the chapters use. Add a new page called **Practice** and build each chart there, next to the finished version for comparison.

text: 1. How Deneb works
1.1 The big picture

Deneb is a Power BI visual that draws whatever you describe in a **specification** (spec) written in one of two languages: **Vega-Lite** (short and high-level, good for most charts) or **Vega** (longer and lower-level, needed for layouts such as packed bubbles, treemaps and maps). Both are JSON: nested `{ "key": value }` objects.

items: You drag columns and measures into the visual's single **Values** well, like any Power BI visual.
Power BI runs the query: it groups by the columns and evaluates the measures in the current filter context (slicers, page filters, cross-filters).
Deneb receives the result as a table called `dataset` and passes it to your spec.
Vega-Lite / Vega draw the chart. When the data changes (a slicer moves), steps 2–4 repeat automatically.

text: 1.2 What `dataset` looks like

For the highlight table in chapter 5 we add **Region**, **SubCategory** and the measure **Total Sales**. Power BI returns one row per Region × SubCategory combination, with the measure already calculated:

text: Three things to notice:

items: **Field names are the display names** from Power BI: `Region`, `SubCategory`, `Total Sales`. Spaces are fine. The characters `. [ ] \ "` are replaced by `_`. If you rename a field in the Values well, the name in the spec must change too.

**Deneb adds helper fields** whose names start with two underscores: `__row__` (row number), `__selected__` (is this row selected?) and, for each measure, `<measure>__highlight` and `<measure>__highlightStatus`. Chapter 4 explains how to use them for interactivity.
**One row per combination of columns.** If you add OrderID as well, you get one row per order. Choose the columns to match the level of detail you want to draw.

text: Let Power BI do the totals with DAX measures, and let the spec do the drawing. Totals calculated by measures respect slicers and filters the same way the rest of the report does, and they keep each drawn mark linked to real rows, which is what makes click-to-filter work.
2. Setting up and the Deneb editor
2.1 One-time setup

items: Open **DenebShowcase.pbip** in Power BI Desktop and click **Refresh** so the tables load.

Check Deneb is installed: you should see its icon at the end of the **Visualizations** pane. If not, use **… → Get more visuals**, search **Deneb**, click **Add** (publisher shown as Daniel Marsh-Patrick).
Add a page: right-click a page tab → **New page** → rename it **Practice**.

text: 2.2 Create a Deneb visual and open the editor

items: Click an empty area of the page, then click the **Deneb** icon. An empty Deneb visual appears.
With the visual selected, tick the fields you need in the **Data** pane (or drag them into **Values**).
Make the visual larger (drag its corner) — the editor preview uses this size.
Click the visual's **…** (More options) → **Edit**. The Deneb editor opens.
The first time, Deneb asks you to create a specification: choose **Vega-Lite** or **Vega**, pick the **empty** template (the one without a pre-built chart), and click **Create**.

text: 2.3 A tour of the editor

rows: Your spec. This is where you type or paste JSON.
Shared styling (fonts, colours, axis look). Kept separate so the spec stays about the chart itself.
Interactivity switches: tooltips, context menu, cross-filtering, cross-highlighting.
Re-draws the preview with your changes. There is also an auto-apply toggle.
The chart, drawn at the visual's real size.
**Data** shows the exact `dataset` rows Deneb received (check field names here!). **Signals** shows Vega signals. **Logs** shows errors and warnings.
Closes the editor. Your spec is saved inside the visual.

text: When a chart is blank, open the **Data** table first: nine times out of ten a field name in the spec doesn't exactly match the name in the table (spelling, spaces or capital letters). Then check **Logs**.
2.4 The working rhythm

items: Start with the smallest spec that draws *something*, then add one thing at a time and press **Apply** after each.
If it breaks, undo the last change (**Ctrl+Z**) and read the error in **Logs**.
JSON is strict: every key in double quotes, commas *between* items but never after the last one, matching `{}` and `[]`. The editor underlines mistakes in red.
Save a copy of a working spec (or use the step files in this guide) before a big change.

text: 3. Vega-Lite in one chapter
Vega-Lite describes a chart with a handful of building blocks. Learn these and you can read any Vega-Lite spec.
3.1 The smallest useful spec

label: A bar chart in 8 lines

caption: What it draws (fields: SubCategory, Total Sales)

rows: Which language and version. Tells the editor how to check your spec. Always the first line.
Where rows come from. In Deneb always `{"name": "dataset"}`.
The shape drawn for each row: `bar`, `line`, `point`, `rect`, `text`, `tick`, `rule`, `area`, `arc`…
Which field controls which visual property (*channel*): position (`x`, `y`), `color`, `size`, `opacity`, `shape`, `text`, `tooltip`…

text: 3.2 Field types
Every encoded field needs a `type`, which decides the kind of scale and axis:

rows: categories with an order (YearMonth as text, PeriodsAgo)
bands in sorted order / colour ramp
continuous axis from a minimum to a maximum

text: 3.3 Mark properties vs encodings

A **mark property** is the same for every row: `"mark": {"type": "bar", "color": "#4e79a7"}`. An **encoding** depends on the data: `"color": {"field": "Category", "type": "nominal"}`. A fixed value inside encoding is written `{"value": ...}`, and a rule-based value uses `condition` (see 3.6).
3.4 Layers

`layer` stacks several marks on the same axes: bars plus a line, rectangles plus text labels, and so on. Anything put in the top-level `encoding` is shared by all layers; each layer adds its own `mark` and extra encodings.

label: Shape of a layered spec

text: When two layers need *different* scales on the same channel (Sales in thousands vs a ratio in %), add `"resolve": {"scale": {"y": "independent"}}`. That is how a Tableau dual axis is built (chapter 6).
3.5 Transforms: calculating inside the spec
`transform` is a list of steps applied to the rows *before* drawing, in order. The ones used in this guide:

rows: adds a new field from an expression
keeps rows where the expression is true
adds a group total to every row (rows are kept)
collapses rows into groups (rows are replaced)
rarely needed — use DAX measures instead

text: In expressions, `datum` is the current row. Use `datum.Region` for simple names and `datum['Total Sales']` for names with spaces or symbols.
3.6 Conditions

label: If the test is true use the first value, otherwise the second

text: 3.7 Scales, axes and legends

items: `scale` controls how data maps to the channel: `{"scheme": "blues"}` for a colour ramp, `{"domain": ["Met", "Missed"], "range": ["#4e79a7", "#e15759"]}` to pin colours, `{"domain": [-45, 45]}` to fix an axis range.
`axis` controls the axis: `title`, `orient` (`top`/`bottom`/`left`/`right`), `format` (`"~s"` = 120k, `".0%"` = 15%), `labelAngle`, `grid`, `labelExpr` (an expression that rewrites each label).
`legend` does the same for legends; `"legend": null` hides it. `"title": null` hides a title.

text: 3.8 Config

`config` sets defaults for the whole chart (fonts, colours, axis styling). In Deneb, put it in the **Config** tab so the spec stays short and the same look can be reused across charts. The Tableau look used in chapters 5–9 is a config — see section 5, step 6.
4. Vega basics and interactivity
4.1 When you need Vega

Vega-Lite *compiles to* Vega. Vega is more verbose because you spell out everything Vega-Lite does for you — scales, axes, marks and data flow — but that also lets you use **layouts** Vega-Lite does not have: circle packing, treemaps, map projections and hierarchical data. Chapters 10, 11, 14 and 15 use Vega.
4.2 The parts of a Vega spec

rows: A list of named datasets. Start with `{"name": "dataset"}` (from Power BI), then derive new datasets with `"source"` + `"transform"`. Each dataset is a step in a pipeline.
Named values or expressions (like variables). `width` and `height` are signals Deneb sets for you.
For maps: how longitude/latitude become x/y (`albersUsa`, `orthographic`, `mercator`…).
Explicit axes and legends (Vega-Lite creates these automatically, Vega does not).
What to draw. Each mark has `type` (`symbol`, `rect`, `text`, `line`, `rule`, `shape`, `group`), `from` (which dataset) and `encode` (how each row sets x, y, fill, size…).

text: Inside `encode`, each property is an object: `{"field": "x"}` reads a field, `{"value": "white"}` is a constant, `{"scale": "color", "field": "Category"}` passes a field through a scale, and `{"signal": "datum.r * 2"}` evaluates an expression. Properties go in `enter` (set once) or `update` (re-evaluated on every change); this guide uses `update` throughout so it is always safe.
4.3 Interactivity: making Deneb behave like a native visual
Three switches and two helper fields give you most of the Power BI behaviour:

headers: What to put in the spec
rows: Vega-Lite: a `tooltip` encoding (list of fields). Vega: a `tooltip` property in `encode`.
Nothing is required: clicking a mark selects its row. To *show* the selection, dim rows where `datum.__selected__ == 'off'`.
Draw `<measure>__highlight` (the highlighted part) on top of a faint copy of the full measure.
Nothing — right-click works on any mark.

text: `__selected__` is `neutral` when nothing is selected, `on` for the selected rows and `off` for the others. `<measure>__highlight` equals the measure when nothing is highlighted, and the highlighted portion when another visual highlights this one. `<measure>__highlightStatus` is `neutral`, `on` or `off` in the same way.

label: The selection pattern used in every chart in this guide

text: Click-to-filter works best when every mark is one row of `dataset`. If the spec merges rows itself (with `aggregate`), Deneb has to guess which rows you clicked by matching field values. It often works, but the reliable approach is to send totals from DAX measures, as all the charts here do.
5. Highlight table (heatmap)

**What you'll build:** a grid of Region × Sub-category where each cell is coloured by sales and shows the number — Tableau's *highlight table*. Clicking a cell filters the page; clicking a Segment bar re-colours the cells to that segment's sales.
Step 1 — Draw the grid
Create a new Vega-Lite spec (empty template), delete everything in the Specification tab and paste:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch05_heatmap_step1.json

text: `rect` draws one rectangle per row of `dataset`. Because `x` and `y` are **nominal** (categories), Vega-Lite splits the width into one band per Region and the height into one band per SubCategory, so the 36 rows become a 4 × 9 grid. Every cell is the same default blue because nothing controls colour yet.
Step 2 — Colour each cell by sales
Change `mark` from a plain string to an object (so it can take properties), and add a `color` encoding:
{"type": "rect", "stroke": "white", "strokeWidth": 1.5}
label: Replace "mark": "rect" with:

text: {"field": "Total Sales", "type": "quantitative", "scale": {"scheme": "blues"}}
label: Add inside "encoding":

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch05_heatmap_step2.json** — paste that file if you get lost.

`color` with a **quantitative** field creates a continuous colour scale and a legend. `"scheme": "blues"` picks a light-to-dark blue ramp (Tableau's default for highlight tables). `stroke` + `strokeWidth` on the mark draw white gaps between cells — a mark property, so it applies to every cell.
Other schemes to try: `greens`, `oranges`, `viridis`, `redblue` (diverging). The full list is on vega.github.io/vega/docs/schemes.
Step 3 — Add the numbers with a second layer
To put text on top of the rectangles we need two marks, so the spec becomes a **layer**. Replace the whole spec with:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch05_heatmap_step3.json

text: The shared `encoding` (x and y) sits at the top level, so both layers use the same grid. Layer 1 is the coloured `rect`; layer 2 is a `text` mark whose `text` channel shows Total Sales. `format: ",.0f"` uses d3-format: thousands separator, no decimals.
We also tidied the axes: `orient: "top"` moves Region labels above the grid like Tableau, `labelAngle: 0` keeps them horizontal, and `title: null` removes the redundant axis titles.
Layers are drawn in order — the first layer is at the back. Put `text` after `rect` or the rectangles will hide the numbers.
Step 4 — Make the numbers readable on dark cells
Dark text disappears on dark blue cells. Add a `transform` (top level, after `data`) and a conditional text colour in the text layer:
[{"joinaggregate": [{"op": "max", "field": "Total Sales", "as": "maxSales"}]}]
label: Add at the top level:
Add inside the text layer's "encoding":

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch05_heatmap_step4.json** — paste that file if you get lost.

`joinaggregate` computes the maximum Total Sales over *all* rows and writes it onto *every* row as `maxSales` — the rows themselves are kept. Now each text mark can compare its own value to the maximum: above 55% of the max the cell is dark, so the text turns white.
This is better than a hard-coded number (like `> 100000`) because it keeps working when slicers change the totals. The legend format `~s` shows 120k instead of 120,000.
Step 5 — Wire up cross-filtering, cross-highlighting and tooltips
Replace the spec with the version below (the differences are explained underneath), then open the **Settings** tab and switch on **Tooltips**, **Cross-filtering** and **Cross-highlighting**.

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch05_heatmap_step5.json

text: **Cross-highlight:** colour and text now use `Total Sales__highlight` instead of `Total Sales`. With nothing highlighted the two are identical; when you click *Consumer* in the Segment bar chart, the highlight field holds only Consumer sales, so the heatmap re-colours to that segment.
**Cross-filter:** clicking a cell selects that row. The `opacity` condition dims every cell whose `__selected__` is `off`, so the clicked cell stands out — exactly like a native visual.
**Tooltip:** a list of fields to show on hover. `title` renames a field in the tooltip; `format` formats numbers.

text: 6. Dual axis: bars + line
**What you'll build:** monthly sales as bars with the profit ratio as a line on a second axis — Tableau's *dual axis* combination chart.

rows: one bar per month (text like 2024-03, sorts correctly)

text: Step 1 — Monthly bars
Create a new Vega-Lite visual with the three fields and paste:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch06_dualaxis_step1.json

text: `YearMonth` is text such as `2024-03`, so we use **ordinal**: categories in sorted order. Text in `YYYY-MM` form sorts alphabetically in date order, which is why the model includes this column.
Step 2 — Add the line — and see the problem
Turn the spec into a layer: the shared x stays on top, each layer brings its own y.

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch06_dualaxis_step2.json

text: The line is there but flat along the bottom. By default layers **share** one y scale, which now runs from 0 to ~80,000; a ratio of 0.15 is invisible on that scale. This is the moment you would drag a second measure onto the right axis in Tableau.
Step 3 — Give each layer its own axis
Add `resolve` at the top level and style both axes:
{"scale": {"y": "independent"}}
label: Add at the top level:
Bar layer:
Line layer:

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch06_dualaxis_step3.json** — paste that file if you get lost.

`"resolve": {"scale": {"y": "independent"}}` gives every layer its own y scale; Vega-Lite automatically puts the second axis on the right. Colouring each axis title like its mark tells the reader which axis belongs to which series. `grid: false` on the line's axis avoids two overlapping sets of gridlines.
Step 4 — Tidy the x-axis and add points
Twenty-four labels are crowded. Show only quarter starts with a label expression, and add dots to the line:

label: Shared x encoding:
Line mark:

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch06_dualaxis_step4.json** — paste that file if you get lost.

`labelExpr` runs for every axis label. `datum.value` is the label text (e.g. `2024-04`); `slice(datum.value, 5)` takes the month part (`04`); `indexof([...], ...) >= 0` checks whether it is a quarter month. If not, the label becomes an empty string. The bars are still all there — only the labels are thinned.
`point` on a line mark draws a dot at each value, which makes individual months easier to hover.
Step 5 — Interactivity: highlight and selection on the bars
Replace with the final spec, then switch on Tooltips, Cross-filtering and Cross-highlighting in **Settings**.

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch06_dualaxis_step5.json

text: The bar layer is now a **nested layer** of two bars on the same y scale: a faint full bar (`opacity: 0.3`) and, on top, a solid bar of `Total Sales__highlight`. When another visual highlights a segment, the solid part shrinks to that segment's share and the faint bar shows the total — Power BI's standard highlight look.

Nesting matters: `resolve` makes the *outer* layers independent (bars vs line), while the two bars inside the nested layer still share one scale. The solid bar's opacity drops to 0 for unselected months, leaving only the faint outline.

text: 7. Bullet graph
**What you'll build:** for each Category, grey bands at 60/80/100/120% of target, a blue bar for actual sales and a black tick at the target — Stephen Few's bullet graph, a Tableau favourite.
Step 1 — A plain bar per category
Paste:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch07_bullet_step1.json

text: Putting the category on `y` makes horizontal bars, which suit long labels.
Step 2 — Add the target tick
Convert to a layer and add a `tick` mark for the target:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch07_bullet_step2.json

text: A `tick` is a short line across the band. `size` is its length (28 px, taller than the bar) and `thickness` its width. The bar's `size: 12` makes it thinner than the band, leaving room for the grey background bands we add next.
Step 3 — Add the qualitative bands
Calculate the band edges, then put four grey bars *before* the existing layers:

label: Add at the top level:
First new layer (the others follow the same pattern; see the step file):

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch07_bullet_step3.json** — paste that file if you get lost.

`calculate` adds `B60`, `B80` and `B120` to each row (60/80/120% of that row's target); 100% is the target itself. Each band is just a wide bar starting at 0, so the **widest (120%) is drawn first** and each narrower, darker band is drawn on top of it. The result looks like adjacent ranges.
Because the bands come from the target measure, they rescale with slicers automatically.
Order matters again: if the 120% band came last it would cover everything else.

text: 9. Bar-in-bar
**What you'll build:** a wide light bar for the target with a narrow bar for actual sales inside it, coloured blue if the target was met and red if missed.
Step 1 — The outer (target) bar
Paste:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch09_barinbar_step1.json

text: `size: 22` sets the bar thickness in pixels so we can later fit a thinner bar inside it.
Step 2 — The inner (actual) bar
Layer a narrower bar for Total Sales on top:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch09_barinbar_step2.json

text: Both bars share the band for each SubCategory and are centred in it, so the 10 px bar sits inside the 22 px one. That is all "bar-in-bar" is.
Step 3 — Colour by status and sort
Add a calculated Status and use it for colour; sort the bars:

label: Top level:

text: {"field": "SubCategory", "type": "nominal", "title": null, "sort": "-x"}
label: Shared y:
Inner bar colour:

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch09_barinbar_step3.json** — paste that file if you get lost.
The `calculate` expression uses the ternary `test ? a : b` operator. Pinning `domain` and `range` guarantees Met is always blue and Missed always red, whatever order the data arrives in.
`"sort": "-x"` sorts the y categories by their x value, descending (the minus sign).

text: 10. Packed bubbles (Vega)

**What you'll build:** one circle per Sub-category, sized by sales and coloured by Category, packed tightly together. Vega-Lite has no packing layout, so this is our first **Vega** spec — re-read section 4.2 first.
Step 1 — Build a hierarchy and pack it
Create a new **Vega** spec (empty template) and paste:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch10_bubbles_step1.json

text: Circle packing needs a **tree**: every node has an `id` and a `parent`. Our rows have no parent, so the `tree` dataset gives every row `id = SubCategory` and `parent = 'root'` with two `formula` transforms.

`rootNode` is a one-row dataset for the top of the tree. `nodes` combines both (`source` can be a list) and runs two transforms: `stratify` links children to parents; `pack` computes `x`, `y` and radius `r` for every node so that circle areas are proportional to `Total Sales` and nothing overlaps.
The `symbol` mark draws a circle per node. Vega's `size` is the symbol's *area* in square pixels, so for a circle of radius r we pass `4 * r * r` (the area of its bounding square).
The big outline circle is the root node — it contains everything. We hide it in step 4.
Dataset names must be unique, and `root` is reserved in Vega, which is why it is called `rootNode`.
Step 2 — Colour by Category, with a legend
Add a `scales` and a `legends` section (top level), and use the scale for `fill`:

text: {"scale": "color", "field": "Category"}

In Vega you create scales yourself. This **ordinal** scale maps each Category (its `domain` is read from the data) to a colour from the `tableau10` scheme. `"fill": {"scale": "color", "field": "Category"}` sends each circle's Category through it. Legends are also explicit: `fill: "color"` builds a legend from that scale.
Step 3 — Labels that fit
Add a second mark — text at each circle's centre:

label: Add to "marks":

`text` is a **signal** (an expression): circles smaller than 16 px radius get an empty label because the name would not fit. `fontSize` grows with the radius but stays between 9 and 14 px. The root has no SubCategory, so its label is empty.
Step 4 — Hide the root, add tooltips and selection
Replace with the final spec (also turn on Tooltips and Cross-filtering in Settings). The key changes are in the circle's `fill`, `fillOpacity` and `tooltip`:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch10_bubbles_step4.json

**Sorting by another field:** `sort: {field: "PeriodsAgo", op: "max", order: "ascending"}` orders the columns by each product's largest PeriodsAgo, i.e. its streak length — short columns on the left, the longest on the right, which creates the staircase.

`paddingInner` on the band scales makes the gaps between tiles (as a fraction of the band). `axis: null` removes the y axis entirely; the x axis is moved to the top without its line or ticks. `cornerRadius` softens the tiles.
Step 3 — Label every tile
Move to a layer (tiles + text) and build the label with a calculate transform:

label: Top level:

`datum.Period + datum.Note` joins two text fields: `2025 Q3` + `*` = `2025 Q3*`. `color` moves into the tile layer only, so the text layer can be white. Bold labels on the blue tiles draw the eye to the quarters that beat target.
Step 4 — Annotate the three longest streaks
Add a `joinaggregate` that finds each product's streak length, and an annotation layer:

label: Add first in "transform":
New layer:

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch12_streak_step4.json** — paste that file if you get lost.
`joinaggregate` with `groupby: ["Product"]` writes each product's maximum PeriodsAgo onto all of its rows as `streakLen`.

The annotation layer has its **own** transforms: keep only the bottom tile of each column (the last "Beat"), rank those by streak length with `dense_rank`, keep the top 3 and build a 3-line note (a text array = one line per item). `align: right` with `dx: -46` places the note to the left of the tile.
Because everything is computed, the annotations move by themselves when the data changes.

Replace with the final spec:

text: The headline is a text layer with its **own inline data** (`data: {values: [...]}`), so it is drawn once rather than once per row. Its position uses pixel values: `x: {value: 0}` and `y: {value: {expr: "height * 0.55"}}` — just over halfway down, whatever size the visual is.
`background` sets the light grey NYT page colour; tiles get a tooltip and the usual selection opacity.

text: `window` with `lag`/`lead` copies the previous and next year's margin onto each row, so an expression can ask "is this bar bigger than both neighbours?" — a local peak. label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch14_usmap_step1.json

text: `format: {type: "topojson", feature: "states"}` tells Vega the values are TopoJSON and to extract the object called `states` as one map feature per state.
A **projection** turns longitude/latitude into x/y. `albersUsa` is a US-specific projection that moves Alaska and Hawaii into insets. `fit` + `size` scale and centre it so the states fill the visual.
The `shape` mark with a `geoshape` transform draws each feature as a path: light grey with white borders. `dataset` is declared but not used yet.

`"autosize": "none"` keeps the chart exactly the size of the visual. Vega's default (`pad`) enlarges the drawing to fit every mark, which for maps and large circles makes the chart spill out of the visual.
Step 2 — Derive airports from the routes
Add three datasets after `states`, and a `symbol` mark:

Datasets `o` and `d` rename the origin and destination columns to the same names (`code`, `name`, `lon`, `lat`). `airports` stacks them (`source: ["o", "d"]`) and `aggregate`s by airport, summing `Cancelled` into `n`: every cancellation counts at both ends of its route.
`geopoint` runs each airport's lon/lat through the projection and adds pixel coordinates `x` and `y`, which the symbol mark uses.

Add a size scale and update the circle style; sort the airports so small ones draw last:

Vega's symbol `size` is an **area**, and readers judge circles by area, so a **linear** scale from 0 makes area proportional to the count: twice the cancellations, twice the ink. (Using radius would exaggerate big airports.)
`collect` sorts the rows by `n` ascending, so the largest circles are drawn first and small ones stay visible on top. Transparent fill with a solid orange edge reproduces the NYT look.

15. Globe with routes (Vega, orthographic)

**What you'll build:** a 3D-looking globe centred on the Indian Ocean, with a shaded ocean, country outlines, hundreds of semi-transparent sea routes that glow where they overlap, red position dots and place labels.

rows: which route a waypoint belongs to
unique id so identical rows are not merged

text: Deneb has a single `dataset`, so routes and positions share one table and the `Kind` column separates them. A route is a sequence of waypoint rows (same `Id`, increasing `Seq`). `RowId` matters: Power BI merges identical rows, and two positions could happen to have the same values.
As in chapter 14, the map outline is pasted in: this time `nyt-style/geo/world_countries.json` (60 KB), shown as `"<contents of world_countries.json>"`.
Step 1 — An orthographic globe
Create a Vega spec with the seven fields and paste:

label: Full spec at this step  ·  tutorial/steps/ch15_globe_step1.json

text: **orthographic** draws the Earth as seen from space. `rotate: [-lon, -lat]` turns the globe so the point (76°E, 10°N) faces you; we keep those numbers in signals so they are easy to change.

`scale` (the zoom) is a signal based on the visual's width, and `translate` puts the globe's centre 62% of the way down, so the top is cropped like the original. `"autosize": "none"` is what allows the cropping: without it Vega would grow the canvas to show the whole sphere (see chapter 14, step 1).

Three layers, drawn in order: the **sphere** (a special GeoJSON type meaning "the whole globe", used as the ocean), a **graticule** (latitude/longitude grid generated by a transform) and the **countries**.
If the whole globe turns white, a country polygon is "inside out" (it happens after simplifying shapes that cross the 180° line, like Fiji). The supplied file has been fixed.
Step 2 — Shade the ocean
Replace the sphere's fill with a radial gradient:
The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch15_globe_step2.json** — paste that file if you get lost.

A radial gradient goes from the centre (`r1`, light) to the edge (`r2`, darker). Coordinates are fractions of the shape's bounding box, so 0.5/0.5 is its centre. The darker rim makes the flat disc read as a sphere.
Step 3 — Draw the routes
Add a `routes` dataset and a **group** mark that draws one line per route:

label: New dataset:
New mark:

text: The complete spec after this step is saved as **tutorial/steps/ch15_globe_step3.json** — paste that file if you get lost.
The dataset keeps only route waypoints, sorts them by route and order (`collect`), and projects them to x/y with `geopoint`.

A single `line` mark would join *all* waypoints into one long line. A **facet group** splits the data by `Id` into one sub-dataset per route (`routeSeg`) and draws the inner `line` mark once for each.

`interpolate: basis` turns the waypoint polyline into a smooth curve. Each line is only 16% opaque, so where dozens of routes overlap the colour builds up into a bright band — the effect in the NYT graphic.

Appendix A — Troubleshooting

rows: A field name in the spec doesn't match `dataset`
Open the editor's **Data** table; copy the exact names (spaces and capitals matter).
JSON syntax: missing or extra comma, unmatched bracket, single quotes around keys
Look at the line before the underline. Keys and text values need double quotes.
Line or bar flat at the bottom
Two layers sharing a y scale with very different ranges
Cross-filtering is off, or the spec aggregates rows
Settings → Cross-filtering; send totals from DAX measures instead of `aggregate`.
Cross-highlighting is off, or the spec doesn't use `<measure>__highlight`
Set the column's *Summarization* to *Don't summarize* in the model.
TopoJSON not inside `values`, wrong `feature` name, or an inside-out polygon
Check `feature` matches the object name in the file (`states`, `countries`).
Only part of the data shows
Visual format → Deneb → **Data limit** → override row limit; or reduce detail.
Text cut off at the edges
Add `padding` at the top level, or shorten labels with `limit`.
